newsitem.title: USA: Family leave becomes U.S. campaign issue.
newsitem.headline: Family leave becomes U.S. campaign issue.

text.p: In a presidential campaign dominated by issues of economics, trust and vision, the concept of family leave briefly took the political spotlight on Saturday.

White House spokesman Barry Toiv confirmed a published report that President Bill Clinton planned to introduce legislation soon that would expand the Family and Medical Leave Act that guarantees workers the right to take unpaid time off during a family medical crisis.

Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole responded by criticising the current law letting workers take unpaid leave to care for a new child or sick family member as too much federal government involvement in private matters.
The back-and-forth came on a day in which Clinton remained out of sight at the White House and Dole took a one-day trip into the swing state of Pennsylvania with stops in Pittsburgh and Wilkes-Barre.

The emphasis on the family appeared at the same time a U.S. News & World Report poll was released showing 49 percent of respondents said Clinton does a better job of addressing concerns of parents raising children than Dole, who rated at 31 percent.

Another new poll showed Clinton continued to ride high in public opinion with his approval rating standing at 61 percent, according to Time/CNN survey released on Saturday. The same poll showed the president's disapproval at 30 percent, the lowest level in almost 3 1/2 years.
In a head-to-head battle Clinton beat Dole 52 to 38 percent with Reform Party candidate Ross Perot at 6 percent.

On the family leave issue, Clinton has called the current law one of his top achievements and plans to ask Congress to expand the reasons for unpaid leave and allow workers to trade overtime pay to compensatory time to meet family obligations.
But White House spokesman Toiv admitted the president had no expectation that the legislation would be approved by Congress but rather wanted to show his support for the idea.
At a question-and-answer session with small business people in Pittsburgh, Dole criticised the current law as unwarranted government intrusion.

"My view is why should the federal government be getting into family leave? It ought to be left to the employees or the state or the county and the federal government ought to be out of it," Dole said.
"I believe in compassionate leave if there is a birth or a death or there is something that happens in a family ... but I again wonder about the long arm of the government," said Dole.
Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart said Dole's stance showed he was resistant to new ideas.
Dole's trip was his third visit to Pennsylvania recently. Polls show him far behind Clinton in this state, which has 23 electoral votes, making it a key battleground.
Dole tried to showcase his economic plan, which calls for a 15 percent income tax cut and halving of the capital gains tax, at a "Listening to America" question-and-answer session.

While Clinton had no public events, he did deliver his weekly radio address, this time calling on the Senate to ratify a global chemical weapons ban treaty that he said would keep poison gas out of the hands of "rogue states like Iraq".
